1.lecture:
§1 · What a punch actually does to sheet

Sheet-metal cutting is not cutting in the machining sense. Nothing is removed as chips: the material is stressed until it fractures along a line the tooling defines. Shearing makes a straight cut, usually to size a strip. Blanking cuts a closed contour and keeps the piece that comes out. Piercing cuts a closed contour and keeps the sheet, throwing away the slug. The mechanics are identical; only the definition of scrap changes, and that difference decides how the tooling is dimensioned.

Follow the punch down and four things happen in order, each leaving its own band on the finished edge. First the material bends into the die opening — rollover, a rounded lip. Then the punch penetrates and the material flows past its edge under compression, producing a smooth, shiny burnished band that is the only part of the edge you would call machined. At some depth the stress reaches the material's limit and cracks start from the punch corner and the die corner; when they meet, the piece separates, leaving a rough, angled fracture zone. Whatever material was dragged rather than cut stands proud as the burr.

An edge is therefore a record of the process that made it, readable without instruments. A wide burnished band with two distinct shiny zones separated by a step means the cracks did not meet and the material was sheared twice. A large rollover and a heavy burr means the opposite. Which of those you get is set almost entirely by one dimension.

§2 · Clearance, and which tool carries the size

Clearance is the gap between punch and die, per side. It is specified as a fraction of the sheet thickness because that is what the crack geometry actually depends on.

Key relation — clearance

\[ c = A_c\,t \]

\( A_c \) is the clearance allowance: roughly 0.045 for soft aluminium, 0.060 for low-carbon steel, 0.075 for stainless and hard alloys — harder and less ductile material needs more.

The clearance's job is to make the two cracks meet. Too little and they miss: the material between them shears a second time, the edge shows a double burnished band, the force rises and the tooling wears faster. Too much and the material is dragged into the gap rather than cut: heavy rollover, a large ragged burr, and a blank that is dished rather than flat. For 3 mm low-carbon steel, \( c = 0.060(3) = 0.18\ \mathrm{mm} \) per side, which is 0.36 mm across a diameter and far larger than most people expect.

That 0.36 mm has to be taken off one tool or added to the other, and the choice is not arbitrary.

Key rule — the product side carries the size

Blanking: the blank is the product, and it takes the size of the die opening. So \( D_{\text{die}} = D \) and \( D_{\text{punch}} = D - 2c \).

Piercing: the hole is the product, and it takes the size of the punch. So \( D_{\text{punch}} = D \) and \( D_{\text{die}} = D + 2c \).

Blanking a \( \varnothing60 \) disc from 3 mm steel therefore needs a 60.00 mm die and a 59.64 mm punch. Piercing a \( \varnothing25 \) hole in the same sheet needs a 25.00 mm punch and a 25.36 mm die. Reverse either rule and every part is 0.36 mm out — a mistake that survives inspection only because it is consistent.

§3 · Force, and how to need less press than the arithmetic says

The force follows from the area actually being sheared, which is the cut perimeter times the thickness.

Key relations — cutting and stripping force

\[ F = S\,t\,L,\qquad S\approx0.7\,\mathrm{TS},\qquad F_{\text{strip}}\approx(0.02\ \text{to}\ 0.10)F \]

\( L \) is the length of the cut, \( t \) the thickness, \( S \) the shear strength. The stripping force pulls the sheet back off the punch after the cut and is carried by the same press stroke, so it belongs in the tonnage sum.

For the \( \varnothing60 \) blank: \( L=\pi(60)=188.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), and with \( \mathrm{TS}=340 \) MPa, \( S=238 \) MPa. Then \( F=238(3)(188.5)=134{,}600\ \mathrm{N} \), which is 134.6 kN, 15.1 US tons, or about 13.7 tonnes force. Adding 5% stripping brings it to 141.3 kN. How the tonnage a press can deliver varies through its stroke is Lesson 5's subject; here the point is only that the number is large and comes almost entirely from the perimeter.

There is a way to need much less of it. Grinding an angular shear onto the tool face means the cut starts at one point and progresses along the contour instead of happening everywhere at once. The total work is unchanged — the same material still has to be separated — but it is spread over a longer punch travel, so the peak force falls.

Key relation — the effect of angular shear

\[ F_{\text{peak}}\approx F\,\frac{p_f t}{p_f t+s} \]

\( s \) is the shear depth ground onto the tool and \( p_f \) is the fraction of the thickness penetrated before fracture, around 0.5 for medium steel. The work \( F\,p_f t \) is conserved; only its distribution over the stroke changes.

With \( t=3 \) mm and \( p_f=0.5 \), a shear of 1.5 mm halves the peak force to 67.3 kN and a shear of 3 mm cuts it to 44.9 kN. The catch is that the tool face is no longer flat, so whatever it pushes on is left distorted — which fixes where the shear goes. In piercing the slug is scrap, so the shear goes on the punch. In blanking the strip is scrap, so the shear goes on the die and the blank comes out flat. Putting it on the wrong member produces a correctly sized, permanently dished product.

§4 · Nesting: the profit nobody watches

In a stamped part the material is commonly half to three-quarters of the cost, and how much of the coil becomes product is decided at the layout stage by a draughtsman, once, for the life of the tool.

Key relations — strip layout

\[ \text{utilisation}=\frac{A_{\text{blank}}}{W\,p/n},\qquad p = D + b,\qquad W = D + 2m\ \ (\text{single row}) \]

\( p \) is the feed pitch, \( b \) the bridge between blanks, \( m \) the web margin at the strip edges, \( n \) the blanks produced per pitch. The bridge and margin are not waste to be minimised freely: they are what holds the strip together through the die, and cutting them too fine tears the carrier.

Take the \( \varnothing60 \) blank with a 3 mm bridge and 3 mm margins. A single row needs a 66 mm strip advancing 63 mm per blank, so each blank consumes \( 66\times63=4{,}158 \) mm² and utilisation is \( 2827/4158=68.0\% \).

Now stagger two rows so the second sits in the gaps of the first. Blanks in adjacent rows are offset half a pitch along the feed, so their centre distance is \( \sqrt{s^2+(p/2)^2} \), and that has to be at least \( D+b \). Solving, \( s=\sqrt{63^2-31.5^2}=54.56\ \mathrm{mm} \) — the rows can be much closer than 63 mm apart because they are also displaced along the strip. The strip becomes \( 60+54.56+6=120.56 \) mm wide and yields two blanks per 63 mm of feed, so each blank consumes 3,798 mm² and utilisation rises to 74.5%.

That is 8.7% less coil per blank. On 3 mm steel it is 8.5 grams a part, 849 kg per hundred thousand, for a change that costs one afternoon at the layout stage and nothing per part thereafter. Three qualifications keep it honest: a wider strip needs a wider press and feed, a staggered layout needs two punches or a two-up die, and any layout that assumes a rectangular blank orientation must be checked against the rolling direction if the part will later be bent — which is the next lesson's problem.
1.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Shear strength, tensile strength, and ductile fracture (Materials Science I L5–L6 and Materials Science II) — why a cut edge shows a burnished band and then a rough one.
  • Stress, plastic deformation, and the yield criterion (Strength of Materials L2–L3) — the material behaviour every relation here rests on.
  • Bulk deformation and press operations (Manufacturing Processes I L7–L9) — the forming family this course continues.
  • Clearance, limits, and how a tolerance is verified (Metrology & Quality Control L5, and Engineering Drawing & CAD L6) — punch and die are a fit, dimensioned like one.

quiz.q:
Size the tools, then the press

Problem. A \( \varnothing60 \) mm disc is blanked from 3 mm low-carbon steel (\( \mathrm{TS}=340 \) MPa, clearance allowance 0.060), and a \( \varnothing25 \) mm hole is pierced in the same sheet. Give the punch and die diameters for both operations. Then find the blanking force, the stripping force at 5%, and the total, in kilonewtons and in US tons.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( c=A_ct=0.060(3.0)=0.18\ \mathrm{mm} \) per side.

(2) Blanking: the blank takes the size of the die opening, so the die is \( \varnothing60.00 \) and the punch is \( 60.00-2(0.18)=\varnothing59.64\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(3) Piercing: the hole takes the size of the punch, so the punch is \( \varnothing25.00 \) and the die is \( 25.00+2(0.18)=\varnothing25.36\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(4) \( S\approx0.7\,\mathrm{TS}=0.7(340)=238\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

(5) \( L=\pi(60)=188.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( F=StL=238(3)(188.5)=134{,}586\ \mathrm{N}=134.6\ \mathrm{kN} \).

(6) \( F_{\text{strip}}=0.05(134.6)=6.73\ \mathrm{kN} \), giving a total of \( 141.3\ \mathrm{kN} \).

(7) In US customary: \( 134{,}586/4.4482=30{,}256\ \mathrm{lbf}=15.13 \) US tons for the cut, and \( 141{,}315/4.4482/2000=15.89 \) US tons in total.

Answer: blanking die \( \varnothing60.00 \), punch \( \varnothing59.64 \); piercing punch \( \varnothing25.00 \), die \( \varnothing25.36 \); 134.6 kN of cutting force plus 6.7 kN stripping, 141.3 kN (15.9 US tons) in total. Sanity check: the two operations put the clearance on opposite members, and the reason is the same in both cases — the product side carries the nominal size. Reversing it gives parts 0.36 mm out on every piece, consistently enough to pass an unwary first-article check. Note that the force depends on the perimeter, not the area: the \( \varnothing25 \) hole needs \( 238(3)(\pi\times25)=56.1 \) kN, less than half the blank's, despite removing less than a fifth of the area.

quiz.q:
Buy the press down with angular shear

Problem. The 134.6 kN blanking operation above is to run on a press rated 100 kN. Taking the penetration fraction at fracture as \( p_f=0.5 \), find the shear depth needed on the tool to bring the peak force under the rating with 20% margin, and the peak force at a shear of 3 mm. State which member the shear is ground onto and why.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The work of separation, \( F\,p_ft \), is fixed. Angular shear spreads it over a punch travel of \( p_ft+s \), so \( F_{\text{peak}}=F\,p_ft/(p_ft+s) \).

(2) Here \( p_ft=0.5(3)=1.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( F_{\text{peak}}=134.6\times1.5/(1.5+s) \).

(3) A 20% margin on a 100 kN press means a target of 80 kN. Setting \( 134.6(1.5)/(1.5+s)=80 \) gives \( 1.5+s=2.524 \), so \( s=1.02\ \mathrm{mm} \). Round up: a 1.5 mm shear gives \( 134.6(1.5)/3.0=67.3\ \mathrm{kN} \), comfortably inside.

(4) At \( s=3 \) mm: \( 134.6(1.5)/4.5=44.9\ \mathrm{kN} \), a third of the flat-tool force.

(5) This is a blanking operation, so the blank is the product and the strip is scrap. The sheared face distorts whatever it presses on, so the shear goes on the die, leaving the blank flat and dishing the scrap strip. In piercing it would go on the punch, because there the slug is the scrap.

Answer: about 1.0 mm of shear meets the 80 kN target and a standard 1.5 mm gives 67.3 kN; 3 mm gives 44.9 kN. The shear is ground on the die, because the blank must stay flat. Sanity check: nothing about the material or the cut length changed, so the total work is the same in every case — only its distribution over the stroke moved, which is exactly why the press requirement fell and the tool life did not improve with it. Note the failure mode this prevents and the one it introduces: it keeps a 134.6 kN cut off a 100 kN press, and it guarantees a dished part if the shear is ground on the wrong member.

quiz.q:
What a layout decision is worth

Problem. The \( \varnothing60 \) blank is to be nested with a 3 mm bridge and 3 mm web margins. Find the strip width, the material consumed per blank and the utilisation for a single row; then for two staggered rows, deriving the row offset. Give the coil saved per blank as a percentage and as a mass, and the annual saving on 100,000 blanks. Take steel at 7.85 g/cm³.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Pitch \( p=D+b=60+3=63\ \mathrm{mm} \); blank area \( A=\pi(60)^2/4=2827\ \mathrm{mm}^2 \).

(2) Single row: \( W=D+2m=60+6=66\ \mathrm{mm} \), so each blank consumes \( 66\times63=4158\ \mathrm{mm}^2 \) and utilisation is \( 2827/4158=68.0\% \).

(3) Staggered rows are offset half a pitch along the feed, so the centre distance between blanks in adjacent rows is \( \sqrt{s^2+(p/2)^2} \), which must be at least \( D+b=63 \). Hence \( s=\sqrt{63^2-31.5^2}=\sqrt{3969-992.25}=54.56\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(4) \( W=60+54.56+6=120.56\ \mathrm{mm} \), and two blanks come off per 63 mm of feed, so each consumes \( 120.56\times63/2=3798\ \mathrm{mm}^2 \) and utilisation is \( 2827/3798=74.5\% \).

(5) Coil saved: \( 1-3798/4158=8.67\% \).

(6) Mass: \( 4158\times3=12{,}474\ \mathrm{mm}^3=12.47\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \), so 97.9 g per blank single-row against \( 3798\times3\times7.85\times10^{-3}=89.4 \) g staggered — 8.49 g saved.

(7) On 100,000 blanks: \( 8.49\times10^5\ \mathrm{g}=849\ \mathrm{kg} \).

Answer: single row 66 mm strip, 4,158 mm² and 68.0%; staggered 120.56 mm strip, 3,798 mm² and 74.5%; 8.67% less coil, 8.5 g per blank, 849 kg per 100,000. Sanity check: the rows sit 54.56 mm apart on a part 60 mm across, which looks impossible until you remember they are also displaced 31.5 mm along the feed — the constraint is the centre distance, not the cross-strip gap, and that is the whole trick. Note what the saving is not: it is not free, because the wider strip needs a wider press and feed and the layout needs two punches. Note also that it is decided once, by a draughtsman, and then repeats on every part for the life of the tool, which is why it deserves an afternoon.

quiz.q: The shiny band on a sheared edge is produced by
choices: the fracture running from the die corner
the punch penetrating and the material flowing past its edge under compression
quiz.solution: That burnished band is the only part of the edge made by anything resembling cutting. Above it sits the rollover where the material first bent into the die, below it the rough fracture zone where cracks from the punch and die corners met, and beyond that the burr. The four zones together are a readable record of the clearance that produced them.

quiz.q: Clearance that is too small produces
choices: a heavy burr and severe rollover
a double burnished band and higher cutting force
quiz.solution: With too little clearance the cracks from the two corners miss each other and the material between them is sheared a second time, leaving two shiny bands with a step between them and raising the force. Heavy burr and rollover are the excessive-clearance signature. Clearance does not change the blank's size — that is set by whichever member is the product side.

quiz.q: To blank a \( \varnothing60 \) mm disc from 3 mm steel with \( A_c=0.060 \), the tools should be
choices: both \( \varnothing60.00 \), with the clearance taken up by tool wear
quiz.solution: In blanking the blank is the product and it takes the size of the die opening, so the die is nominal and the punch is smaller by \( 2c=0.36 \) mm. The first option is the piercing rule applied by mistake, and it would make every disc 0.36 mm oversize — consistently enough to survive a careless inspection.

quiz.q: Doubling the diameter of a blanked disc, at constant thickness, changes the cutting force by a factor of
quiz.solution: \( F=StL \) and \( L \) is the perimeter, so force scales with diameter, not with area. This is why a long thin slot can need more tonnage than a large round hole, and why adding a decorative outline to a stamping is not free.

quiz.q: In a blanking operation the angular shear should be ground onto the
choices: punch, because it carries the load
die, because the strip is the scrap and the blank must stay flat
either, since the effect is the same
quiz.solution: A sheared tool face distorts whatever it presses on. In blanking the product is the blank and the scrap is the strip, so the shear goes on the die. In piercing the slug is the scrap, so it goes on the punch. Putting it on the wrong member gives a correctly sized and permanently dished product.

quiz.q: Staggering two rows of \( \varnothing60 \) blanks at a 63 mm pitch lets the rows sit 54.56 mm apart because
choices: the blanks are allowed to overlap slightly
adjacent-row blanks are also offset half a pitch along the feed, so their centre distance is \( \sqrt{s^2+(p/2)^2} \)
the bridge is not needed between rows
quiz.solution: The constraint is the centre-to-centre distance, not the cross-strip gap. With a 31.5 mm offset along the feed, a 54.56 mm row spacing still gives \( \sqrt{54.56^2+31.5^2}=63 \) mm between centres. It is why staggering works at all, and why the saving grows with how round the blank is.

quiz.q: Moving the \( \varnothing60 \) blank from a single row to staggered double rows takes utilisation from 68.0% to 74.5%. The coil saved per blank is
quiz.solution: Utilisation rose by 6.5 percentage points, which is a 9.5% relative rise, but what the shop buys is coil: \( 1-3798/4158=8.67\% \) less steel per blank. Reporting the percentage point difference understates it and the utilisation ratio overstates it — the quantity that appears on an invoice is the area consumed.

quiz.q: The bridge and web margin in a strip layout exist to
choices: give the press feed something to grip and hold the strip together through the die
allow for thermal expansion of the coil
quiz.solution: They are the carrier: the strip has to survive being fed, located and stripped after each station, and a bridge cut too fine tears. That is why utilisation cannot simply be driven toward 100% by shrinking them, and why the real gains come from the layout geometry instead.

1.kuwait:
Applied case — the tool that was ordered from the wrong rule. A fabricator ordered a blanking tool for a \( \varnothing60 \) mm disc in 3 mm steel. The tool arrived with a \( \varnothing60.00 \) punch and a \( \varnothing60.36 \) die. First-article inspection measured the blanks at \( \varnothing60.34 \) against a \( \varnothing60\ \pm0.2 \) drawing, and because every part measured the same the shop concluded the process was capable and released it. The discs were rejected at assembly.

The tool had been dimensioned by the piercing rule. In blanking the blank is the product and it takes the size of the die opening, so the die should have been \( \varnothing60.00 \) and the punch \( \varnothing59.64 \). Sized the other way, every disc came out roughly \( 2c=0.36 \) mm oversize — consistently, which is exactly why it passed a check that looked at spread rather than at position. Metrology & Quality Control makes the same point from the other side: a process can be in perfect control and stably wrong, and a capability index compares the process with the tolerance, not with itself.

Two practices follow. State on the tool drawing which member is nominal and why, in words rather than only in numbers — "die nominal, blank is the product" is one line and it removes the entire failure mode. And treat a first article that is consistently offset as the most suspicious result available: consistency is evidence about the spread and says nothing at all about whether the tooling was built to the right rule.
1.recap:
• Sheet cutting separates by fracture, not by chip removal: shearing, blanking and piercing share the mechanics and differ only in which side is scrap.
  • A cut edge carries four zones in order — rollover, burnish, fracture, burr — and is a readable record of the clearance that made it.
  • \( c=A_ct \), with \( A_c \) about 0.045 for soft aluminium, 0.060 for low-carbon steel and 0.075 for hard alloys; on 3 mm steel that is 0.18 mm per side.
  • Too little clearance double-shears and raises force; too much drags, rolls over and burrs.
  • The product side carries the size: blanking die \( =D \) and punch \( =D-2c \); piercing punch \( =D \) and die \( =D+2c \).
  • \( F=StL \) with \( S\approx0.7\,\mathrm{TS} \) — a \( \varnothing60 \) blank in 3 mm steel needs 134.6 kN, plus about 5% stripping, so 141.3 kN or 15.9 US tons.
  • Force scales with the cut perimeter, so a long thin feature can cost more tonnage than a large round one.
  • Angular shear spreads the same work over a longer stroke: \( F_{\rm peak}\approx F\,p_ft/(p_ft+s) \), so 1.5 mm of shear halves 134.6 kN to 67.3 kN. It goes on the die for blanking and the punch for piercing.
  • Staggered rows sit \( s=\sqrt{(D+b)^2-(p/2)^2}=54.56 \) mm apart because they are also offset half a pitch along the feed.
  • That single layout decision takes utilisation from 68.0% to 74.5% — 8.7% less coil, 8.5 g per blank, 849 kg per 100,000 — for one afternoon's work at the drawing stage.

2.lecture:
§1 · The flat length is not the sum of the legs

Bend a strip and the outer surface stretches while the inner one is compressed. Somewhere between them is a surface whose length does not change — the neutral axis — and the flat blank has to be cut to the length of that, not to the sum of the finished legs. Get it wrong and every part is short or long by a few millimetres, consistently, on a tool that is otherwise perfect.

The neutral axis does not sit at mid-thickness. Material thins on the tensile side more than it thickens on the compressive side, so the neutral surface migrates inward, and the migration depends on how sharp the bend is. Shops carry that in a single factor.

Key relation — bend allowance

\[ \mathrm{BA}=2\pi\frac{\alpha}{360}\bigl(R+K t\bigr),\qquad K\approx0.33\ (R<2t),\qquad K\approx0.50\ (R\ge2t) \]

\( \alpha \) is the swept bend angle, \( R \) the inside radius, \( t \) the thickness. \( K \) is where the neutral axis sits, as a fraction of the thickness measured from the inside surface.

For a 90° bend with \( R=6 \) mm in \( t=3 \) mm sheet, \( R/t=2 \) so \( K=0.50 \), and \( \mathrm{BA}=2\pi(0.25)(6+1.5)=11.78\ \mathrm{mm} \). Draughtsmen more often work with the bend deduction, because parts are dimensioned to their outside faces:

Key relation — bend deduction

\[ \mathrm{BD}=2(R+t)\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}-\mathrm{BA} \]

Flat length = (sum of outside dimensions) − (one BD per bend). The first term is the outside setback: how far the outside faces would run past each other if the corner were sharp.

Here \( \mathrm{BD}=2(9)(1)-11.78=6.22\ \mathrm{mm} \). A U-channel with outside dimensions 50 + 80 + 50 = 180 mm and two 90° bends therefore develops to \( 180-2(6.22)=167.56\ \mathrm{mm} \) of flat blank. Use \( K=0.33 \) by mistake — the value for a tight bend, on a bend that is not tight — and the blank comes out 165.96 mm: 1.6 mm short on a part nobody would suspect, because both bends and both legs are individually correct. The arithmetic is unit-blind, so the same bend at \( R=0.25 \) in and \( t=0.125 \) in gives \( \mathrm{BA}=0.4909 \) in, which is the 12.47 mm the metric calculation would have given.

§2 · Springback: the bend that opens after the punch lifts

Bending strains the outer fibres past yield, but not all of the strain is plastic. When the load comes off, the elastic component recovers and the bend opens: the angle decreases and the radius grows. This is springback, and it is not a defect — it is elasticity doing what elasticity does.

Key relation — springback

\[ \frac{R_i}{R_f}=4\left(\frac{R_i Y}{E t}\right)^{3}-3\left(\frac{R_i Y}{E t}\right)+1 \]

Everything material-dependent enters through \( Y/E \) — yield strength over elastic modulus. A stronger material springs back more; a stiffer one springs back less; and the two effects are of equal weight.

That answers the question shops ask most often. High-strength steel springs back more than mild steel not because it is "harder" but because it has the same \( E \) and nearly three times the \( Y \): at \( R/t=10 \), a 90° bend recovers 3.3° in mild steel and 9.1° in high-strength steel. Aluminium 6061-T6 has a lower yield than that high-strength steel — 275 MPa against 700 — and springs back further still, 10.7°, because its modulus is 69 GPa against steel's 207. Ranking materials by strength predicts springback badly; ranking them by \( Y/E \) predicts it correctly.

Note the other variable in the bracket: \( R_i/t \). Springback grows with it, which is why the same material behaves quite differently in different operations. A tight bend at \( R/t=2 \) barely moves; a wide air bend at \( R/t=20 \) recovers 6.5° in mild steel and 21.3° in aluminium — a quarter of the angle asked for.

Four responses exist and shops use all of them. Overbending is the cheapest: bend past the target by the predicted recovery, so a mild-steel bend aimed at 90° is formed to \( 90/0.9638=93.4^{\circ} \). Bottoming presses the sheet fully into the die so the bend zone yields through its thickness, and coining goes further and sets the radius plastically — both reduce springback and both cost force, coining several times more than air bending. Stretch forming superimposes tension so the whole section is plastic, nearly eliminating springback, and is why aircraft skin panels are formed that way. And an adaptive press brake measures the angle mid-stroke and corrects, which is the only one of the four that copes with sheet whose yield varies from coil to coil.

§3 · Force, and a question with two right answers

V-die bending force comes from treating the sheet as a beam loaded at the punch and supported at the die shoulders.

Key relation — bending force

\[ F=\frac{K_{bf}\,\mathrm{TS}\,w\,t^{2}}{D} \]

\( w \) is the length of the bend, \( D \) the die opening, and \( K_{bf}\approx1.33 \) for a V-die or 0.33 for a wiping die. The thickness appears squared and the die opening divides.

For a 1 m bend in 3 mm steel of 340 MPa with the usual \( D=8t=24 \) mm opening, \( F=1.33(340)(1000)(9)/24=169.6\ \mathrm{kN} \) — 19.1 US tons per metre of bend, or 5.8 tons per foot.

Now the question worth being careful with: what happens when the sheet thickness doubles? If the die opening is left alone, force goes as \( t^2 \) and quadruples to 678 kN. But nobody leaves the die opening alone — it is chosen as a multiple of thickness, so \( D=8t \) grows too, and \( F\propto t^2/t=t \): the force merely doubles, to 339 kN. Both answers are correct and they differ by a factor of two, so the question is incomplete until someone says whether the tooling changed. It is also the reason a press brake's tonnage chart is published against die opening rather than against thickness alone.

One more limit belongs here. Bend a material tighter than it can stretch and the outer fibre cracks. The usable minimum radius follows from the tensile reduction of area \( r \), in per cent: \( R_{\min}/t = 50/r - 1 \). A steel with \( r=40\% \) can be bent to \( R=0.25t \); one with \( r=20\% \) needs \( R=1.5t \). It is a ductility measurement doing duty as a forming specification.

§4 · Direction, sequence, and the tolerance the drawing should ask for

Rolled sheet is not isotropic. Rolling elongates grains and stretches inclusions into stringers along the rolling direction, so the material is weaker across those stringers than along them. A bend line parallel to the rolling direction stretches the outer fibre across the stringers and cracks at a radius the same material tolerates easily when the bend line runs perpendicular. The practical rule is that \( R_{\min} \) is roughly one and a half to two times larger for a bend line along the rolling direction, and the fix is free: rotate the part on the strip. For a part with bends on two axes, one of them will be unfavourable, and the layout has to decide which bend gets the larger radius — which is why Lesson 1's nesting decision cannot be made on utilisation alone.

Two more shop realities shape the drawing. Bend sequence is constrained by tool access: a flange formed early can collide with the ram or the die on a later bend, so the order is planned backwards from the last bend, and a part that cannot be sequenced has to be redesigned rather than argued about. And a bend that stops partway along an edge tears at its ends unless a small relief notch is cut in the flat pattern first — a feature that costs nothing at the blanking stage and cannot be added afterwards.

Finally, what to write on the drawing. A brake-formed angle holds about \( \pm0.5^{\circ} \) routinely and \( \pm0.25^{\circ} \) with in-process angle measurement; a developed flat length holds about \( \pm0.25 \) mm. Those figures are the process talking, and a drawing that asks for \( \pm0.1^{\circ} \) is asking for a different process, not for more care. Metrology & Quality Control makes the same point from the measuring side — a tolerance is only meaningful against a process that can hold it and a gauge that can see it.
2.foundations:
What this lesson assumes

  • Elastic and plastic behaviour, yield strength and the elastic modulus (Materials Science I L4–L5, Strength of Materials L2) — springback is the elastic part of the strain coming back.
  • Bending stress and the neutral axis of a beam (Strength of Materials L4) — the same neutral surface, now permanently deformed.
  • Reduction of area from the tensile test (Materials Science I L5) — used directly as \( R_{\min}/t=50/r-1 \).
  • Rolling and the anisotropy it creates (Manufacturing Processes I L8) — why the bend line's direction matters.
  • Blanking, clearance and strip layout (Lesson 1) — the flat pattern and the relief notches are cut there.
  • Achievable tolerance versus a specified one (Metrology & Quality Control L5 and L8) — what a drawing may reasonably ask of a press brake.

quiz.q:
Develop the flat blank

Problem. A U-channel is formed from 3 mm sheet with two 90° bends at an inside radius of 6 mm. Its outside dimensions are 50, 80 and 50 mm. Find the bend allowance, the bend deduction and the flat blank length. Then find the error if \( K=0.33 \) had been used instead, and give the bend allowance for the same geometry stated as \( R=0.25 \) in in 0.125 in sheet.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( R/t=6/3=2 \), which is not less than 2, so \( K=0.50 \).

(2) \( \mathrm{BA}=2\pi\frac{90}{360}(6+0.5\times3)=\frac{\pi}{2}(7.5) =11.78\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(3) Outside setback \( =(R+t)\tan45^{\circ}=(6+3)(1)=9.0 \) mm, so \( \mathrm{BD}=2(9.0)-11.78=6.22\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(4) Flat length \( =(50+80+50)-2(6.22)=180-12.44=167.56\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(5) With \( K=0.33 \): \( \mathrm{BA}=\frac{\pi}{2}(6+0.99)=10.98 \) mm, \( \mathrm{BD}=18-10.98=7.02 \) mm, flat \( =180-14.04=165.96 \) mm — 1.60 mm short.

(6) In inches: \( R/t=0.25/0.125=2 \), so \( K=0.50 \) again and \( \mathrm{BA}=\frac{\pi}{2}(0.25+0.0625)=0.4909\ \mathrm{in} \), which is 12.47 mm — the same bend, since \( 0.25 \) in is 6.35 mm rather than 6.00.

Answer: BA 11.78 mm, BD 6.22 mm, flat 167.56 mm; using \( K=0.33 \) makes the blank 1.60 mm short; the inch geometry gives BA 0.4909 in. Sanity check: the flat is shorter than the sum of the outside dimensions and longer than the sum of the inside ones, which is the only sensible place for it — the corner material has to go somewhere. Note how the 1.60 mm error hides: both bends are the right angle, both legs are the right length, and only the overall developed length is wrong, so it survives every check except measuring the finished part end to end.

quiz.q:
Three materials, one bend

Problem. A 90° bend is formed at \( R_i/t=10 \) in three materials: mild steel (\( Y=250 \) MPa, \( E=207 \) GPa), high-strength steel (\( Y=700 \) MPa, \( E=207 \) GPa) and aluminium 6061-T6 (\( Y=275 \) MPa, \( E=69 \) GPa). Find \( Y/E \) and the springback in degrees for each, rank them, and give the overbend angle needed for the mild steel. Explain why the ranking is not the ranking by yield strength.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( Y/E \): \( 250/207000=1.21\times10^{-3} \); \( 700/207000=3.38\times10^{-3} \); \( 275/69000=3.99\times10^{-3} \).

(2) With \( x=(R_i/t)(Y/E) \) and \( R_i/R_f=4x^3-3x+1 \):

(3) Mild steel: \( x=10(1.208\times10^{-3})=0.01208 \), so \( R_i/R_f=4(1.76\times10^{-6})-0.03623+1=0.9638 \) and the bend opens by \( 90(1-0.9638)=3.26^{\circ} \).

(4) High-strength steel: \( x=0.03382 \), \( R_i/R_f=0.8987 \), springback \( 9.12^{\circ} \).

(5) Aluminium: \( x=0.03986 \), \( R_i/R_f=0.8807 \), springback \( 10.74^{\circ} \).

(6) Ranking, least to most: mild steel, high-strength steel, aluminium. By yield strength the ranking would be mild steel, aluminium, high-strength steel — aluminium and the high-strength steel swap places, because aluminium's modulus is a third of steel's and the governing group is \( Y/E \), not \( Y \).

(7) Overbend for mild steel: form to \( 90/0.9638=93.38^{\circ} \), which recovers to \( 93.38\times0.9638=90.0^{\circ} \).

Answer: \( Y/E \) = 1.21, 3.38, 3.99 \( \times10^{-3} \); springback 3.26°, 9.12° and 10.74°; overbend the mild steel to 93.38°. Sanity check: a material that yields late and springs back stiffly recovers little, and both halves of that sentence carry equal weight — which is exactly why the aluminium, with the lowest strength of the two non-mild materials, springs back the most. Note the practical consequence: a press-brake program written for mild steel and run on 6061-T6 will produce bends about 7° open, and no amount of care at the machine will fix it without changing the target angle.

quiz.q:
Tonnage, and a question with two right answers

Problem. A 1 m long 90° bend is air-formed in 3 mm steel of \( \mathrm{TS}=340 \) MPa in a V-die opened to \( 8t \), with \( K_{bf}=1.33 \). Find the force in kilonewtons, in US tons per metre and in US tons per foot. Then find the force if the thickness doubles to 6 mm, (a) with the die opening unchanged and (b) with the die opening also scaled to \( 8t \), and say which answer a press-brake tonnage chart is built around.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( D=8t=24\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( F=\dfrac{1.33(340)(1000)(3)^2}{24}=\dfrac{1.33(340)(9000)}{24} =169{,}575\ \mathrm{N}=169.6\ \mathrm{kN} \).

(2) \( 169{,}575/4.4482=38{,}122\ \mathrm{lbf}=19.06 \) US tons per metre, which is \( 19.06\times0.3048=5.81 \) US tons per foot.

(3) (a) Die opening fixed at 24 mm: \( F\propto t^2 \), so \( F=1.33(340)(1000)(36)/24=678{,}300\ \mathrm{N}=678.3\ \mathrm{kN} \) — four times.

(4) (b) Die opening scaled to \( 8t=48 \) mm: \( F=1.33(340)(1000)(36)/48=339{,}150\ \mathrm{N}=339.2\ \mathrm{kN} \) — twice, because \( F\propto t^2/D \) and \( D\propto t \) leaves \( F\propto t \).

(5) A tonnage chart is published against die opening precisely because of this: the answer is not determined by the material and thickness alone.

Answer: 169.6 kN, 19.06 US tons per metre, 5.81 per foot; doubling the thickness gives 678.3 kN at a fixed die opening and 339.2 kN with the opening scaled — a factor of four or of two, depending on the tooling. Sanity check: both answers are right and they differ by a factor of two, so the question as usually asked is under-specified. The physical reason is worth holding: a wider die opening is a longer beam span, and a longer span needs less force for the same bend — at the price of a larger formed radius, which then increases springback by §2's relation. Nothing in sheet forming is adjusted in isolation.

quiz.q: The flat blank for a bent part is developed from
choices: the sum of the outside dimensions
the sum of the inside dimensions
the arc length of the neutral axis through each bend, added to the flat legs
the sum of the legs plus twice the thickness per bend
quiz.solution: The neutral surface is the one whose length does not change, so the blank must carry its arc length: \( \mathrm{BA}=2\pi\frac{\alpha}{360}(R+Kt) \). Expressed against outside dimensions this becomes the bend deduction, which is what a draughtsman usually subtracts — 6.22 mm per bend for a 90° bend at R6 in 3 mm sheet.

quiz.q: The factor \( K \) in the bend allowance is smaller for tight bends because
choices: the neutral axis migrates toward the inside surface
the bend angle is measured differently
the radius is harder to measure
quiz.solution: The outer fibre thins more than the inner fibre thickens, so the surface of unchanged length moves inward — roughly 0.33t from the inside for \( R<2t \) against 0.50t for gentler bends. Using 0.50 where 0.33 belongs, or the reverse, puts every blank out by a millimetre or two while leaving all the angles and legs correct.

quiz.q: Springback is governed by
quiz.solution: The springback relation depends on the material only through \( x=(R_i/t)(Y/E) \). A stronger material springs back more and a stiffer one springs back less, with equal weight — which is why 6061-T6 aluminium, at 275 MPa, springs back further than a 700 MPa steel: its modulus is a third as large.

quiz.q: At \( R/t = 10 \), a 90° bend in mild steel springs back about 3.3°. The same bend in aluminium 6061-T6 springs back about
quiz.solution: \( Y/E \) is \( 3.99\times10^{-3} \) against mild steel's \( 1.21\times10^{-3} \), roughly 3.3 times, and the springback follows: 10.74°. A press-brake program written for mild steel and run on 6061-T6 leaves every bend about 7° open, and care at the machine cannot recover it.

quiz.q: Springback increases with \( R/t \). The practical consequence is that
choices: tight bottomed bends hold their angle better than wide air bends
thicker sheet always springs back more
quiz.solution: \( x=(R_i/t)(Y/E) \), so a wide air bend at \( R/t=20 \) recovers 6.5° in mild steel where a tight bend at \( R/t=2 \) barely moves. It is the main reason bottoming and coining are used where angle accuracy matters, despite costing several times the force.

quiz.q: V-die bending force is \( F=K_{bf}\mathrm{TS}\,wt^{2}/D \). If the sheet thickness doubles and the die opening is scaled to \( 8t \) as usual, the force
quiz.solution: \( F\propto t^2/D \), and scaling \( D\propto t \) leaves \( F\propto t \), so 169.6 kN becomes 339.2 kN. Only if the die opening is left unchanged does the force quadruple to 678.3 kN. Both answers are correct and the question is incomplete without the tooling — which is why tonnage charts are published against die opening.

quiz.q: A steel with a tensile reduction of area of 20% has a minimum bend radius of about
quiz.solution: \( R_{\min}/t=50/r-1=50/20-1=1.5 \). It is a ductility measurement from the tensile test doing duty as a forming specification. A more ductile steel at \( r=40\% \) manages \( 0.25t \), and the same material bent along the rolling direction needs one and a half to two times more.

quiz.q: A bend line running parallel to the rolling direction
choices: is preferred, since the grain supports the bend
needs a larger minimum radius, because the outer fibre stretches across the inclusion stringers
makes no difference in modern steels
quiz.solution: Rolling stretches inclusions into stringers along the rolling direction, and bending parallel to them pulls the outer fibre across them, so cracking starts at a radius the same sheet tolerates easily the other way round. The fix costs nothing — rotate the part on the strip — which is why the layout of Lesson 1 cannot be settled on utilisation alone.

2.kuwait:
Applied case — the panel run that changed material and not the program. A fabricator formed roof and wall panels on a press brake to a program developed and proven on mild steel. A contract specified the same profiles in a high-strength grade, at the same thickness and the same nominal dimensions, and the program was reused unchanged on the reasonable-sounding grounds that the geometry had not moved. The first panels came off with every bend several degrees open, the profiles would not interlock, and the batch was scrapped.

Nothing had gone wrong at the machine. Springback depends on the material only through \( Y/E \), and the new grade had the same modulus as mild steel with nearly three times the yield, so at the profile's \( R/t \) the bends recovered roughly three times as far — about 9° instead of 3°. The program's overbend was compensating for the old material's recovery, and against the new one it was simply the wrong number. Worse, the substitution was invisible on the drawing: the geometry, thickness and tooling were all unchanged, and the only thing that moved was a material property nobody had been asked to check.

Two practices follow. Treat a material change as a tooling change: the overbend is part of the process specification, not a property of the part, and it must be re-derived from \( Y/E \) and re-proven on a sample before a run. And where a shop forms several grades on one tool, prefer a strategy that does not depend on knowing the material — bottoming, or an adaptive brake that measures the angle mid-stroke — because coil-to-coil variation in yield within a single grade is enough to move a bend by a fraction of a degree even when nothing has been substituted.
2.recap:
• The flat blank carries the arc length of the neutral axis, not the sum of the legs: \( \mathrm{BA}=2\pi\frac{\alpha}{360}(R+Kt) \).
  • The neutral axis migrates inward on tight bends: \( K\approx0.33 \) for \( R<2t \) and \( 0.50 \) for \( R\ge2t \). Using the wrong one puts a two-bend part 1.6 mm out while every angle and leg stays correct.
  • Bend deduction \( =2(R+t)\tan(\alpha/2)-\mathrm{BA} \); a 50/80/50 U-channel at 90°, R6, t3 develops to 167.56 mm.
  • Springback is elastic recovery: \( R_i/R_f=4x^3-3x+1 \) with \( x=(R_i/t)(Y/E) \) — the material enters only as \( Y/E \).
  • At \( R/t=10 \) a 90° bend recovers 3.3° in mild steel, 9.1° in high-strength steel and 10.7° in 6061-T6 aluminium, which ranks differently from yield strength alone.
  • Springback grows with \( R/t \) too, which is why tight bottomed bends hold their angle and wide air bends do not.
  • Four compensations: overbend (93.4° for 90° in mild steel), bottoming, coining and stretch forming — plus adaptive brakes, the only approach that copes with coil-to-coil variation.
  • \( F=K_{bf}\mathrm{TS}\,wt^2/D \) gives 169.6 kN per metre at t3 in a 24 mm die — 19.1 US tons per metre, 5.8 per foot.
  • Doubling the thickness quadruples the force at a fixed die opening and only doubles it when the opening is scaled to \( 8t \); tonnage charts are published against die opening for that reason.
  • \( R_{\min}/t=50/r-1 \) from the tensile reduction of area, and a bend line along the rolling direction needs 1.5 to 2 times more radius — a free fix if the layout is decided before the tool is cut.
